en: The one you contest is Chinmachin;
The enemy you oppose is Bakburchun;
The one you fight is Kakan-Chyn.
Will a young man not die while grappling?
Will he not see the decree
Almighty God has written for his entrusted life!
Does a man not go against the foe
And struggle to take revenge?
The road of holy war is a great road;
Is it right to turn back?
You grapple with the many Chinese;
Can you avoid fighting to the death,
Tearing lungs and taking gall?
Extend your spear, break the host,
And return having avenged your lion father Manas!”
If fate reaches you, fall to a bullet!
Does a hero not die at an enemy's hand?
Ah, my gray wolf Semetey,
Will those who remain not live out their days!
Beijing is that formidable stronghold;
If you face it, do not remain alive.
Kongurbai, khan of Beijing,
Is the lion who slaughtered your father.
The son of the great lion said:
"Is it right to fear war?
Can there be a man who will not fight?
Unless you pull down the golden pillar
Of hero Kongurbai's tent,
Unless you tear out its pillar,
Unless you finish him and unleash strife,
Lion Manas went to the other world;
Unless you avenge him,
May you sink without offspring,
And, never being called Manas's son,
May you die rather than live!
The reason I speak thus is this:
Did mighty Manas not gather
The whole world under his rule?
Did he not ask the one Almighty Allah,
Saying, 'Grant me a son who will avenge me,'
And receive you in answer!
Break the Chinese and seize their migration;
If you are a man, my only one,
For your father gone to the other world,
Take vengeance upon Kongurbai!
The prince's only son—
Without campaigning against Beijing,
Is it right for him to wander grieving,
Without fighting against Kakan?
Can this behavior of yours be right?
Your father Manas was a lion;
Almighty Allah will never
Create and grant another mortal
Like your father!
The father of your father Manas, the gray wolf,
Yakyp, was driven away,
And Manas was born in Altai.
When he reached eight years,
He killed twelve boys
Among the Black Kalmaks and Manchus,
And threw those people into turmoil.
At nine he stood firm;
When he reached exactly ten,
He pressed down and devoured
Every mortal who faced him.
When he reached eleven,
There was Esen Khan's envoy,
His appointed frontier scout,
Who stood at the blood-red throne,
A master jeweler of many wonders,
The swaggering champion of the Kalmaks,
Named Döngö,
Esen Khan's treasury wrestler.
Yesterday, when he came to oppress
The Kyrgyz of forty households,
Saying, 'We shall drive away
All wealthy Yakyp's countless cattle;
Esen Khan requires them,'
When Döngö came from China,
When hero Döngö with his whole force
Brought grievous hardship,
When he raided all the countless cattle
And drove them away in confusion,
Hero Manas on Toruchaar,
At twelve years of age,
Confronted them in Altai;
Your lion Manas, the gray wolf,
Unleashed an upheaval.
There in Altai
He wrought utter turmoil;
With hero Döngö at their head,
On that campaign in Altai
He slew two thousand champions.
Before Esen Khan,
The fugitives reported
That he had slain two thousand wrestlers.
Hearing this news, Esen Khan
Gave him the name "Bloodthirsty."
The noble lion had humiliated
Their merchants
And oppressed those who came.
His deeds are far too many to name;
Shall I go on recounting
More deeds like those?
It is well known that
Lord Manas the lion was a hero.
Shielding the Kyrgyz even from the wind,
It is well known that mighty Lord Manas
Was their fortress.
Would no male child be born from Manas?
If he is truly his son,
Will he not pursue his father's blood-price!
Does a son not die for his father?
If he is truly a hero,
Will Semetey, the hero's son,
Not go to Beijing and return!
My golden spring in the valley,
My young champion, son of lion Manas,
Whom I beheld late in life.
For your father Manas the lion,
For the hero gone to the other world,
Break the enemy ranks with your spear;
Let them call you "the doomed man's son,"
And if death comes, fall to a bullet!
If you have the means, my only one,
Seize Kongurbai, khan of the monks,
That swaggering scoundrel,
And bring him back from the ford;
Will your vengeance not then be sated?
Bring him and offer him as a sacrifice!
Drag him along the road
And have the Dangyts tear him apart!
Cut off his head and bind it on,
So the sorrow within me may ease;
Bring it to Sarykan!
The traveler takes a migration;
The tiger among mortals takes revenge.
When he sets out, he brings good fortune,
And against the foe is like a countless host.
May God guide your road;
May the spirit of your tiger father,
My orphan, uphold you!
May Kongurbai, the foe you will grapple with,
My orphan, be weaker than you!
When you level your spear toward him,
When you make holy war upon China,
May Almambet, Chubak, and hero Syrgak,
Those lions, be your companions!
Lean forward and spear the warriors;
If your heroic gray-wolf father supports you,
Spear fifty of them in a single rank!
Turn your spear-fight into autumn harvest;
Raze to the ground the city
Of the wandering Black Chinese!
My young champion, son of Manas,
Now is your time to show heroism
Against the Black Chinese you confront!
My young champion, son of the Bloodthirsty One,
Now is your time to wreak havoc
Upon the hostile Black Chinese!
You brave youth born of Manas,
Go and bring a great upheaval
Upon the Black Chinese you confront!"
Sarykan spoke many words;
Then Sarykan ceased.
After Sarykan,
The lame smith Bölökbai spoke—
While Lord Manas lived,
His nobility was beyond measure.
A star stirred in the heavens;
Bölökbai and David
Were friends through twelve journeys.
To put the matter briefly,
The noble smith Bölökbai
Was encountered through the unseen;
Dear smith Bölökbai
Was found in his youth
By lion Manas himself.
From every kind of material,
Guns that fired and sharp swords,
He made perfectly
For his companion Manas, the gray wolf.
He was his father's companion,
His surpassing smith and confidant.
Among round-headed mortals,
For noble Manas's hand
He forged and distributed arkesken blades.*
Almighty Allah
Had created your poor Bölökbai
As a man surpassing others.
Know his excellence from this:
For Lord Manas, the gray wolf,
He joined what was broken
And gathered what was scattered.
For glorious Manas,
He built houses as he traveled,
And planted gardens as he journeyed.
He brought all this about by his skill
And filled all his chests
With treasures of yellow gold.
He made his tent-cover rich with fat;
Whenever Manas came to him,
He readied every piece of his equipment.
He fitted Kylbolot* into its sheath,
And for the Forty Companions, forty spears,
Joining on their keen iron points
That felled every enemy who challenged them.
He made the spears splendid to behold;
Saying, "Ah, my poor Bölökbai,"
Manas had a thousand broodmares
From his herds driven to him as an allotment.
Bölökbai, inherited as a legacy
From grandfather Manas the gray wolf,
Was both a lord and a lion;
From Manas who passed before,
The lame smith Bölökbai
Was that hero left as a legacy.
The lame smith Bölökbai
Said this to Semetey:
"The Kakanchin are those you will fight;
My only one, you have undertaken
A holy campaign against Kakan.
Bakburchun are those you will confront;
You stand saying that you will go,
My only one born of a valiant man,
And have set out on campaign to Beijing.
When Bölökbai, Bakai, and Sarykan
Have all come to old age,
You abandon your uncles desolate!
May your journey be one of battle;
A campaign to Beijing requires arms and equipment.
I knew that you would strike
Kakanchin's Beijing;
I knew that you would bring
Turmoil upon China.
Knowing this, I myself prepared it,
So that when Semetey went on campaign
He might coil it around his arm and hang it there—
This work of his lame ritual father.
So that he might know its worth,
So that in Beijing of Chin-Machin
He might enter the true battle...
I have a wonder to tell of:
This one axe of mine
Is worth six hundred broodmares.
Its socket is steel and its point is sharp;
I had gold drawn over its handle.
I sharpened its edge and sheathed it;
I had its edge honed hair-fine.
In the venom of a dragon
I tempered it sixty times.
I made the battle-axe ready;
Not for one year,
But for six years without pause I prepared it.
I knew that in Kakanchin's Beijing
You would pursue the blood-price.
